cards.name: Clavicle
cards.etymology: From Latin clavicula ‘little key’, diminutive of clavis ‘key’. Probably because it rotates along its long axis like a key turning in a lock (or resembles an ancient key). So it means ‘the little key bone’.
articulations: Costal cartilage of rib 1 (via costoclavicular ligament)
cards.tip: The most commonly fractured bone, usually at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds; the only bony link between arm and trunk.

cards.name: Femur
cards.etymology: Latin femur ‘thigh’. So it simply means ‘the thigh bone’.
cards.tip: The longest and strongest bone; neck fractures in older adults can cut off the blood supply to the head.

cards.name: Frontal bone
cards.etymology: From Latin frons, frontis ‘forehead, front’. So it means ‘the forehead bone’ — it forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits.
cards.tip: Two halves fuse in early childhood; a persistent midline metopic suture is a normal variant.

cards.name: Hip bone (os coxae)
cards.etymology: Os coxae is Latin ‘bone of the hip’ (coxa ‘hip’). It fuses from three bones: ilium, from Latin ilia ‘flanks, loins’; ischium, from Greek ischion ‘hip joint, haunch’; and pubis, from Latin (os) pubis, from pubes ‘grown-up, adult’ — named for the hair that appears over it at puberty. So: the flank part, the sitting/haunch part and the ‘adult’ part.
landmarks: Ilium: iliac crest, ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, PSIS dimples, iliac fossa, gluteal lines, auricular surface
Ischium: ischial tuberosity (sit bone), ischial spine, ischial ramus
Pubis: pubic tubercle, pubic crest, symphyseal surface, superior and inferior pubic rami
Acetabulum (all three bones meet here at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage)
cards.tip: The ischial tuberosity is the hamstrings’ origin; the ASIS is the origin of sartorius and the standard landmark for pelvic tilt.

cards.name: Humerus
cards.etymology: From Latin umerus ‘shoulder, upper arm’ (the h was added later). So it means ‘the shoulder/upper-arm bone’.
cards.tip: Surgical-neck fractures endanger the axillary nerve; mid-shaft fractures the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

cards.name: Occipital bone
cards.etymology: From Latin occiput ‘back of the head’, from ob ‘against, behind’ + caput ‘head’. So it means ‘the bone at the back of the head’.
cards.tip: Upper trapezius, semispinalis capitis and the suboccipitals attach around the nuchal lines — the ‘yes’ nod happens at its condyles on C1.

cards.name: Parietal bone
cards.etymology: From Latin paries, parietis ‘wall’ (of a house). So it means ‘the wall bone’ — the paired bones form the side walls and roof of the cranium.
cards.tip: Temporalis takes origin from the temporal fossa below the temporal lines on this bone.

cards.name: Patella
cards.etymology: Latin patella ‘small dish, small pan’, diminutive of patina ‘dish’. So it means ‘the little dish’ — a flat, rounded plate at the front of the knee.
landmarks: Lateral and medial articular facets (lateral larger)
cards.tip: The largest sesamoid bone, in the quadriceps tendon; it lengthens the quads’ lever arm for knee extension.

cards.name: Scapula
cards.etymology: Latin scapula ‘shoulder blade’ (classically used in the plural scapulae ‘the shoulders’); probably related to a root meaning ‘to dig’, likening it to a spade. So it means ‘the shoulder blade’.
cards.tip: Seventeen muscles attach to it — rotator cuff, deltoid, traps, rhomboids, serratus anterior, biceps, triceps long head and more.

cards.name: Sternum — body
cards.etymology: Sternum from Greek sternon ‘chest, breast’. The body was historically called the gladiolus (Latin ‘small sword’, the blade of the sword-shaped sternum). So it means ‘the blade of the breastbone’.
articulations: Costal cartilages of ribs 2 (in part) to 7 (sternocostal joints)
cards.tip: CPR compressions go on the lower half of the sternal body — above the xiphoid.

cards.name: Tibia
cards.etymology: Latin tibia ‘shin bone’, also ‘flute, pipe’ — probably because early flutes were made from animal shin bones. So it means ‘the shin bone’.
cards.tip: Its anterior border lies just under the skin — the ‘shin’ — which is why shin fractures are often open.

cards.name: Biceps brachii
cards.etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps, ‘two-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the arm’.
cards.origin: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle of scapula and superior glenoid labrum; short head: apex of the coracoid process of scapula
cards.insertion: Radial tuberosity, and via the bicipital aponeurosis into the deep fascia of the medial forearm
cards.tip: Biceps reflex tests C5–C6; it is a powerful supinator — think of turning a screwdriver clockwise with the right hand.

cards.name: Deltoid
cards.etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder.
cards.origin: Lateral third of clavicle (anterior border), lateral margin and superior surface of acromion, and inferior lip of the spine of the scapula
cards.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
actions: Shoulder abduction (acromial part, beyond the first ~15°)
Shoulder flexion and internal rotation (clavicular part)
Shoulder extension and external rotation (spinal part)
cards.tip: Shoulder dislocations or surgical-neck fractures can injure the axillary nerve — check sensation over the “regimental badge” area and deltoid strength.

cards.name: Gastrocnemius
cards.etymology: From Greek gastēr ‘belly’ + knēmē ‘leg, shin’. So it means ‘the belly of the leg’ — the bulging calf muscle.
cards.origin: Medial head: posterior femur above the medial condyle; lateral head: lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle
cards.insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
cards.tip: Joins soleus to form the Achilles tendon (triceps surae); crosses the knee, so stretch it with the knee straight.

cards.name: Gluteus maximus
cards.etymology: From Greek gloutos ‘buttock’ + Latin maximus ‘largest’. So it means ‘the largest buttock muscle’ — the big superficial mass that shapes the buttock.
cards.origin: Posterior ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, dorsal surface of sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, thoracolumbar fascia
cards.insertion: Iliotibial tract (most fibres) and gluteal tuberosity of femur
actions: Stabilises the knee in extension via the IT tract
cards.tip: Most active in powerful extension from flexion (stairs, squat lock-out, sprinting) rather than in level walking.

cards.name: Latissimus dorsi
cards.etymology: From Latin latissimus ‘widest’ (superlative of latus, broad) + dorsi ‘of the back’ (dorsum). So it means ‘the widest muscle of the back’ — the broadest muscle sheet in the body.
cards.origin: Spinous processes of T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia, posterior iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, often the inferior angle of scapula
cards.insertion: Floor of intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
cards.tip: Prime mover in pull-ups, lat pulldowns and the swimming stroke; tight lats limit overhead reach and pull the lumbar spine into extension when arms go overhead.

cards.name: Pectoralis major
cards.etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it).
cards.origin: Clavicular head: anterior surface of medial half of clavicle; sternocostal head: anterior surface of sternum and costal cartilages 1–6; abdominal part: aponeurosis of external oblique (anterior rectus sheath)
cards.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus (crest of greater tubercle)
actions: Shoulder extension from a flexed position (sternocostal head)
cards.innervation: Lateral pectoral nerve (C5–C7) and medial pectoral nerve (C8–T1)
cards.tip: Its tendon twists so the lower fibres insert highest — ruptures usually happen at the bottom of a heavy bench press.

cards.name: Rectus abdominis
cards.etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the straight muscle of the belly’ — its fibres run straight up and down.
cards.origin: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis
cards.insertion: Xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5–7
cards.tip: The ‘six-pack’ comes from tendinous intersections; separation of the two bellies at the linea alba is diastasis recti, common postpartum.

cards.name: Rectus femoris
cards.etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’ (femur, thigh). So it means ‘the straight muscle of the thigh’ — its fibres run straight down the front of the thigh, unlike the oblique vasti.
cards.origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head); superior acetabular rim (reflected head)
cards.insertion: Base of patella via the quadriceps tendon, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
cards.tip: The only quad that crosses the hip — stretch it with hip extension + knee flexion.

cards.name: Trapezius
cards.etymology: From Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapeza, table), source of ‘trapezium/trapezoid’. Left and right trapezius together form a big trapezoid (four-sided diamond) shape over the upper back.
cards.origin: External occipital protuberance, medial third of superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae, spinous processes of C7–T12
cards.insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion and spine of scapula
actions: Cervical extension and contralateral rotation (upper fibres)
cards.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
cards.tip: Upper and lower traps form a force couple with serratus anterior for upward rotation — essential for pain-free overhead pressing.

cards.name: Triceps brachii
cards.etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’.
cards.origin: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of scapula; lateral head: posterior humerus above (lateral to) the radial groove; medial head: posterior humerus below (medial to) the radial groove
cards.insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (and deep fascia of forearm)
cards.tip: Triceps reflex tests C7; the long head crosses the shoulder, so overhead extensions stretch it most.

cards.name: Calcaneus
cards.etymology: From Latin calx, calcis ‘heel’ (also ‘lime, chalk’). So it means ‘the heel bone’.
landmarks: Medial and lateral processes of the tuberosity (plantar fascia)
cards.tip: The largest tarsal; the Achilles tendon inserts on its tuberosity and plantar fasciitis pain sits at its medial process.

cards.name: Fibula
cards.etymology: Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’. Probably because the slender fibula beside the tibia looks like the pin of a brooch. So it means ‘the pin bone’.
articulations: Talus (lateral malleolus, part of the ankle joint)
cards.tip: Biceps femoris and the LCL attach to its head; the common fibular nerve wraps around its neck, where it is easily injured.

cards.name: Mandible
cards.etymology: From Latin mandibula ‘jaw’, from mandere ‘to chew’. So it means ‘the chewing bone’ — the movable lower jaw.
cards.tip: The only freely movable skull bone (besides the ossicles); temporalis inserts on the coronoid process, masseter on the ramus and angle.

cards.name: Maxilla
cards.etymology: Latin maxilla ‘jaw, jawbone’, a diminutive related to mala ‘cheek, jaw’. So it means ‘the (upper) jaw bone’.
cards.tip: Holds the upper teeth and the largest paranasal sinus; it is fixed — all chewing motion comes from the mandible.

cards.name: Radius
cards.etymology: Latin radius ‘spoke of a wheel, ray’. So it means ‘the spoke’ — in pronation and supination it swings around the ulna like a spoke around a hub.
cards.tip: Thumb-side forearm bone; a fall on an outstretched hand classically breaks its distal end (Colles fracture).

cards.name: Sacrum
cards.etymology: From Latin os sacrum ‘sacred bone’, a translation of Greek hieron osteon. Why it was ‘sacred’ is uncertain — probably because it was the part offered in sacrifices, or thought to be indestructible. So it means ‘the sacred bone’ at the back of the pelvis.
articulations: Ilium of each hip bone (sacroiliac joints)
cards.tip: The dimples of Venus mark the posterior superior iliac spines — the SI joints lie just deep to them, at about S2.

cards.name: Sternum — manubrium
cards.etymology: Sternum from Greek sternon ‘chest’; manubrium is Latin ‘handle’. The sternum was likened to a sword, so it means ‘the handle of the breastbone’.
articulations: Costal cartilage of rib 2 (in part, at the sternal angle)
cards.tip: Find the sternal angle and slide sideways to locate rib 2 — the standard way to count ribs.

cards.name: Temporal bone
cards.etymology: From Latin tempus, temporis ‘time’, via tempora ‘the temples’. Probably because the temples are where grey hair first shows the passage of time (the exact origin is uncertain). So it means ‘the bone of the temple’.
landmarks: Petrous part (houses middle and inner ear)
cards.tip: The mastoid process is the insertion of sternocleidomastoid — palpate it just behind the earlobe.

cards.name: Ulna
cards.etymology: Latin ulna ‘elbow, forearm’ (related to English ‘ell’, an old forearm-length measure). So it means ‘the elbow bone’ — its olecranon is the point of the elbow.
articulations: Triquetrum and lunate indirectly, via the articular disc (TFCC)
cards.tip: Little-finger-side forearm bone; the olecranon is the point of the elbow you lean on, and the hook of the trochlear notch makes it the elbow’s main hinge.

cards.name: Zygomatic bone
cards.etymology: From Greek zygōma ‘bar, bolt’, from zygon ‘yoke’. So it means ‘the yoke bone’ — it yokes the face to the side of the skull via the zygomatic arch.
cards.tip: The cheekbone; masseter arises from the zygomatic arch.

cards.name: Adductor longus
cards.etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ (ad ‘to’ + ducere ‘to lead’) + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long muscle that draws the leg in’ toward the midline.
cards.origin: Body of the pubis, just below the pubic crest
cards.insertion: Middle third of the linea aspera of the femur
cards.tip: The most commonly strained adductor in ‘groin strains’; its tendon is the prominent cord you feel at the groin.

cards.name: Anterior deltoid (clavicular part)
cards.etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder. ‘Clavicular’ is from Latin clavicula ‘little key’ — the part arising from the collarbone.
cards.origin: Anterior border and superior surface of lateral third of clavicle
cards.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
cards.tip: Heavily loaded by pressing (bench, overhead press) — usually needs less isolation work than the middle and posterior delts.

cards.name: Biceps femoris
cards.etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps ‘two-headed’) + femoris ‘of the thigh’. So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the thigh’ — long and short heads join into one tendon.
cards.origin: Long head: ischial tuberosity; short head: lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line
cards.insertion: Head of the fibula
cards.innervation: Sciatic nerve: tibial division (long head) and common fibular division (short head) (L5–S2)
cards.tip: The lateral hamstring — its tendon is the cord on the outside back of the knee, and it’s a frequent site of sprinting strains.

cards.name: Diaphragm
cards.etymology: From Greek dia ‘across, through’ + phragma ‘fence, partition’ (phrassein, to fence in). So it means ‘the partition across’ — the dome-shaped wall between chest and abdomen.
cards.origin: Sternal part: back of xiphoid; costal part: inner surfaces of lower 6 costal cartilages and ribs; lumbar part: crura on L1–L3 bodies and medial/lateral arcuate ligaments
cards.insertion: Central tendon
actions: Inspiration (contracts and descends, enlarging thoracic cavity)
cards.tip: ‘C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive’; diaphragmatic (belly) breathing and 360° bracing use it to build intra-abdominal pressure that stabilises the spine.

cards.name: External oblique
cards.etymology: From Latin externus ‘outer’ + obliquus ‘slanting’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the outer slanted abdominal muscle’ — its fibres slant down and forward.
cards.origin: External surfaces of ribs 5–12
cards.insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior half of iliac crest (lower edge forms the inguinal ligament)
cards.tip: Fibres run ‘hands in pockets’; the right external oblique pairs with the left internal oblique to rotate the trunk to the left.

cards.name: Gluteus medius
cards.etymology: From Greek gloutos ‘buttock’ + Latin medius ‘middle’. So it means ‘the middle buttock muscle’ — middle in size and depth, between maximus and minimus.
cards.origin: External surface of ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines
cards.insertion: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
actions: Stabilises the pelvis in single-leg stance
Hip internal rotation and flexion (anterior fibres)
Hip external rotation and extension (posterior fibres)
cards.tip: Weakness gives a positive Trendelenburg sign — the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the weak leg.

cards.name: Internal oblique
cards.etymology: From Latin internus ‘inner’ + obliquus ‘slanting’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the inner slanted abdominal muscle’ — fibres slant up and forward, at right angles to the external oblique.
cards.origin: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior two-thirds of iliac crest, lateral half of inguinal ligament
cards.insertion: Inferior borders of ribs 10–12, linea alba, and pubic crest/pecten via conjoint tendon
cards.innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal (T12), iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
cards.tip: Rotates to the same side (unlike the external oblique); trained with Pallof presses, cable chops and side planks.

cards.name: Lower trapezius (ascending part)
cards.etymology: Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapezoid shape); ‘ascending’ because its fibres ascend from the lower thoracic spine up to the scapular spine.
cards.origin: Spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of T4–T12 (approximately)
cards.insertion: Medial end (tubercle) of spine of scapula
cards.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
cards.tip: Commonly weak in scapular dyskinesis and shoulder impingement — prone Y-raises are the classic strengthening drill.

cards.name: Middle deltoid (acromial part)
cards.etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder. ‘Acromial’ is from Greek akron ‘tip’ + ōmos ‘shoulder’ — the part arising from the acromion, the tip of the shoulder.
cards.origin: Lateral margin and superior surface of acromion
cards.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
actions: Shoulder abduction (prime mover after the first ~15°)
Shoulder abduction in the scapular plane
cards.tip: Multipennate, so it is strong but short-ranged; lateral raises train it, and supraspinatus helps initiate abduction.

cards.name: Middle trapezius (transverse part)
cards.etymology: Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapezoid shape); ‘transverse’ from Latin transversus ‘turned across’ — its fibres run horizontally across from the spine to the scapula.
cards.origin: Spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of C7–T3 (approximately)
cards.insertion: Medial border of acromion and superior lip of spine of scapula
actions: Stabilises scapula against chest wall during arm movements
cards.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
cards.tip: Train with prone T-raises and wide-grip rows with a deliberate squeeze of the shoulder blades.

cards.name: Pectoralis major — clavicular head
cards.etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it). ‘Clavicular’ is from Latin clavicula ‘little key’ — the head arising from the collarbone.
cards.origin: Anterior surface of medial half of clavicle
cards.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
cards.tip: Emphasised by incline pressing and low-to-high cable flyes, because its fibres run upward toward the clavicle.

cards.name: Posterior deltoid (spinal part)
cards.etymology: From Greek delta (the triangular letter Δ) + -eidēs ‘shaped like’ (via Latin deltoides). So it means ‘the triangle-shaped muscle’ — an inverted Δ capping the shoulder. ‘Spinal’ refers to the spine of the scapula (Latin spina ‘thorn’), from which this part arises.
cards.origin: Inferior lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula
cards.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
cards.tip: Often underdeveloped relative to the front delts — face pulls and reverse flyes help balance pressing-dominant programmes.

cards.name: Semimembranosus
cards.etymology: From Latin semi ‘half’ + membranosus ‘membranous’. So it means ‘the half-membrane muscle’ — its upper part is a flat, sheet-like tendon.
cards.origin: Ischial tuberosity (superolateral impression)
cards.insertion: Posterior surface of the medial tibial condyle; expansions form the oblique popliteal ligament
cards.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
cards.tip: Lies deep to semitendinosus; its expansions also tension the posterior knee capsule and medial meniscus.

cards.name: Semitendinosus
cards.etymology: From Latin semi ‘half’ + tendinosus ‘tendinous’. So it means ‘the half-tendon muscle’ — its lower half is a long, cord-like tendon.
cards.origin: Ischial tuberosity (common tendon with the long head of biceps femoris)
cards.insertion: Superior medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
cards.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
cards.tip: Back tendon of the pes anserinus (‘Say Grace before Tea’) and a common ACL reconstruction graft.

cards.name: Serratus anterior
cards.etymology: From Latin serratus ‘saw-toothed’ (serra, saw) + anterior ‘in front’. So it means ‘the saw-toothed muscle at the front (side) of the chest’ — its rib slips look like saw teeth.
cards.origin: External surfaces of the lateral parts of ribs 1–8 (often 1–9)
cards.insertion: Anterior (costal) surface of the medial border of the scapula, from superior to inferior angle
actions: Holds the scapula against the thoracic wall
cards.tip: Long thoracic nerve injury causes medial scapular winging; the “plus” phase of a push-up-plus trains it.

cards.name: Soleus
cards.etymology: From Latin solea ‘sandal, sole’ (also the flatfish ‘sole’). So it means ‘the sole-shaped muscle’ — a broad, flat muscle under the gastrocnemius, probably named for its flatfish shape.
cards.origin: Posterior head and upper shaft of the fibula, soleal line and medial border of the tibia, tendinous arch between them
cards.insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
actions: Ankle plantarflexion (dominant when the knee is flexed)
Postural control of standing (prevents forward sway)
cards.tip: Doesn’t cross the knee — target it with bent-knee calf raises and stretches; with gastrocnemius it forms the Achilles tendon.

cards.name: Sternocleidomastoid
cards.etymology: From Greek sternon ‘chest/breastbone’ + kleis, kleidos ‘key’ (the clavicle) + mastoeidēs ‘breast-shaped’ (mastos ‘breast’ + eidos ‘form’). So it means ‘the sternum-and-clavicle-to-mastoid muscle’ — named exactly for its three attachments.
cards.origin: Sternal head: anterior surface of manubrium; clavicular head: superior surface of medial third of clavicle
cards.insertion: Lateral surface of mastoid process and lateral half of superior nuchal line
actions: Head/neck rotation to the opposite side (unilateral)
Accessory inspiration (elevates sternum when head is fixed)
cards.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C2–C3
cards.tip: Tight, overactive SCM goes with forward-head posture; to stretch the right SCM, laterally flex left and rotate the head right with slight extension.

cards.name: Tibialis anterior
cards.etymology: From Latin tibia ‘shin bone’ (originally ‘flute’) + -alis ‘relating to’ + anterior ‘front’. So it means ‘the front shin-bone muscle’ — it lies along the front of the tibia.
cards.origin: Lateral condyle and upper half to two-thirds of the lateral surface of the tibia; interosseous membrane
cards.insertion: Medial and plantar surfaces of the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal
cards.tip: Overload causes anterior shin splints; weakness (e.g. deep fibular nerve palsy) gives foot drop. Anterior ankle order: ‘Tom Has A Very Nervous Eating Disorder’.

cards.name: Transversus abdominis
cards.etymology: From Latin transversus ‘turned across’ + abdominis ‘of the abdomen’. So it means ‘the cross-wise abdominal muscle’ — fibres run horizontally round the belly like a corset.
cards.origin: Internal surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral third of inguinal ligament
cards.insertion: Linea alba, pubic crest and pecten pubis via conjoint tendon
actions: Tensions thoracolumbar fascia to stabilise lumbar spine and pelvis
cards.innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal (T12), iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
cards.tip: The body’s ‘corset’: delayed TrA activation is seen in low back pain; cue drawing-in for isolation, then progress to full bracing for heavy lifts.

cards.name: Upper trapezius (descending part)
cards.etymology: Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (trapezoid shape); ‘descending’ because its fibres descend from the skull and neck down to the shoulder.
cards.origin: External occipital protuberance, medial third of superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae
cards.insertion: Lateral third of clavicle
cards.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C3–C4
cards.tip: Often overactive and tight (shrugging during presses, desk posture); cue ‘shoulders down’ and strengthen lower trap to rebalance.

cards.name: Vastus lateralis
cards.etymology: From Latin vastus ‘vast, huge’ + lateralis ‘of the side’. So it means ‘the huge muscle on the outer side’ — the largest quadriceps head, on the lateral thigh.
cards.origin: Greater trochanter, upper intertrochanteric line, gluteal tuberosity and lateral lip of the linea aspera
cards.insertion: Lateral border of the patella and quadriceps tendon, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
cards.tip: Largest quad head; a strong VL relative to VMO can pull the patella laterally.

cards.name: Vastus medialis
cards.etymology: From Latin vastus ‘vast, huge’ + medialis ‘of the middle (inner) side’. So it means ‘the huge muscle on the inner side’ — the teardrop-shaped quad above the medial knee.
cards.origin: Lower intertrochanteric line, spiral line, medial lip of the linea aspera and medial supracondylar line
cards.insertion: Medial border of the patella and quadriceps tendon, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
actions: Medial stabilisation of the patella (oblique fibres, VMO)
cards.tip: Its lower oblique fibres (VMO) resist lateral patellar tracking — a classic focus in patellofemoral pain rehab.

cards.name: 12th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The twelfth costa — a floating rib (vertebral) and atypical.
articulations: Anterior end free in the posterior abdominal wall
landmarks: Shortest of the lower ribs (length varies a lot)
No tubercle, no angle, no costal groove
Attachment of quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm (lateral arcuate ligament region)
cards.tip: Quadratus lumborum pulls down on it in forced expiration; the kidney and pleura lie just in front of it.

cards.name: 1st rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The first costa — a true rib (vertebrosternal) and atypical. True ribs reach the sternum by their own cartilage; false ribs do not; floating ribs have no front attachment.
articulations: T1 body (costovertebral joint — single facet on the head)
landmarks: Shortest, broadest and most curved rib; flat with superior and inferior surfaces
Groove for subclavian vein (in front of the tubercle)
Groove for subclavian artery and lower brachial plexus trunk (behind the tubercle)
cards.tip: Lies largely behind the clavicle; a cervical rib or tight scalenes here can cause thoracic outlet syndrome.

cards.name: Atlas (C1)
cards.etymology: Named after Atlas, the Greek Titan who held up the heavens on his shoulders. So it means ‘the bone that holds up the globe of the head’.
articulations: Axis (median atlanto-axial joint with the dens, and lateral atlanto-axial joints — rotation ‘no’)
cards.tip: A ring of bone with no body; its large transverse process can be felt between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible.

cards.name: Axis (C2)
cards.etymology: From Latin axis ‘axle, pivot’. So it means ‘the pivot’ — the atlas and head rotate around its dens like a wheel on an axle.
cards.tip: About half of all neck rotation happens at C1–C2; its large spinous process is the first bony bump felt below the occiput.

cards.name: C7 vertebra (vertebra prominens)
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ from Latin cervix ‘neck’; prominens is Latin ‘projecting’ — named for its long, easily felt spinous process.
landmarks: Long, non-bifid spinous process (ends in a tubercle)
Small transverse foramina (vertebral artery usually enters at C6, not C7)
cards.tip: The most prominent spinous process at the base of the neck — the usual starting point for counting vertebrae (T1 can be equally prominent; C7 slides forward under your finger on neck flexion-extension).

cards.name: Coccyx
cards.etymology: From Greek kokkyx ‘cuckoo’. So it means ‘the cuckoo bone’ — its tapering shape was likened to a cuckoo’s beak.
cards.tip: The tailbone: gluteus maximus, coccygeus and levator ani (via the anococcygeal body) attach to it.

cards.name: Hyoid bone
cards.etymology: From Greek hyoeidēs ‘shaped like the letter upsilon (υ)’. So it means ‘U-shaped bone’ — exactly its shape in the front of the neck.
articulations: No bony articulation — suspended by muscles and the stylohyoid ligaments
cards.tip: Sits at about C3; anchor for the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles that move it during swallowing.

cards.name: L5 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the fifth vertebra of the loin (low back).
articulations: Sacrum (lumbosacral joint: L5–S1 disc and facets)
Ilium (via iliolumbar ligament, not a synovial joint)
landmarks: Largest lumbar body, wedge-shaped (taller in front)
Massive transverse processes joined to the ilium by the iliolumbar ligament
cards.tip: Its wedge shape creates the lumbosacral angle; L5 is the commonest site of spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis, and L4–L5/L5–S1 discs herniate most often.

cards.name: Nasal bone
cards.etymology: From Latin nasus ‘nose’. So it means ‘the nose bone’ — the paired bones form the bony bridge of the nose.
landmarks: Lower border attaching the lateral nasal cartilages
cards.tip: The most commonly fractured facial bone — a ‘broken nose’ is usually these.

cards.name: Scaphoid
cards.etymology: From Greek skaphē ‘boat, skiff’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘boat-shaped bone’ — its concave surface was likened to a small boat. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Tubercle (palpable at the wrist crease, base of thenar eminence)
cards.tip: The most commonly fractured carpal; snuffbox tenderness after a fall needs imaging, as waist fractures risk avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.

cards.name: Sphenoid bone
cards.etymology: From Greek sphēn ‘wedge’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — it is wedged into the middle of the skull base between the other cranial bones.
cards.tip: Butterfly-shaped keystone of the skull base; the lateral pterygoid plate anchors the pterygoid chewing muscles.

cards.name: Sternum — xiphoid process
cards.etymology: From Greek xiphos ‘sword’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘the sword-shaped process’ — the pointed tip of the sword-like sternum.
landmarks: Pointed tip, cartilaginous in youth (ossifies around age 40)
Attachment of the sternal part of the diaphragm
Attachment of rectus abdominis (anterior surface, with cartilages 5–7)
cards.tip: Keep your hands off it in CPR — compressing the xiphoid can injure the liver.

cards.name: Talus
cards.etymology: Latin talus ‘ankle bone, knucklebone’ — ankle bones of animals were used as dice. So it means ‘the ankle bone’. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Posterior process with medial and lateral tubercles
cards.tip: No muscles attach to it; its trochlea is wider in front, so the ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion.

cards.name: Adductor brevis
cards.etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short muscle that draws the leg in’ — shorter than adductor longus, which lies in front of it.
cards.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
cards.insertion: Pectineal line and upper part of the linea aspera of the femur
cards.tip: Lies between the anterior and posterior divisions of the obturator nerve — a useful landmark.

cards.name: Adductor magnus
cards.etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ + magnus ‘great, large’. So it means ‘the great muscle that draws the leg in’ — the largest adductor, filling the back of the medial thigh.
cards.origin: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus; hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
cards.insertion: Adductor part: gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera and medial supracondylar line; hamstring part: adductor tubercle of the femur
cards.innervation: Obturator nerve (adductor part, L2–L4); tibial division of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part, L4)
cards.tip: Dual nerve supply because its hamstring part acts like a hamstring; the femoral vessels pass through its adductor hiatus.

cards.name: Anterior scalene
cards.etymology: From Greek skalēnos ‘uneven, unequal’ (as in a scalene triangle with unequal sides) + Latin anterior ‘front’. So it means ‘the front uneven muscle’ — the scalenes are three unequal muscles that together form a lopsided triangle on the side of the neck.
cards.origin: Anterior tubercles of transverse processes of C3–C6
cards.insertion: Scalene tubercle on inner border of 1st rib
actions: Slight cervical rotation to the opposite side
cards.tip: Thoracic outlet: the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between anterior and middle scalenes (subclavian vein passes in front), so a tight anterior scalene can compress them; the phrenic nerve lies on its front.

cards.name: Biceps brachii — long head
cards.etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps, ‘two-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘long head’ has the longer tendon, running from above the glenoid through the shoulder joint.
cards.origin: Supraglenoid tubercle of scapula and superior glenoid labrum (tendon runs intra-articularly then down the intertubercular groove)
cards.insertion: Radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis (common tendon with short head)
actions: Stabilises the humeral head (depresses it in the glenoid)
cards.tip: Site of SLAP lesions and bicipital tendinopathy in the groove; a rupture gives the “Popeye” bulge. Incline curls stretch it.

cards.name: Biceps brachii — short head
cards.etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps, ‘two-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘short head’ has the shorter tendon, arising from the coracoid process.
cards.origin: Apex of the coracoid process of scapula (with coracobrachialis)
cards.insertion: Radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis (common tendon with long head)
cards.tip: Shares the coracoid origin with coracobrachialis and pec minor’s insertion; preacher and spider curls (arm in front) bias it.

cards.name: Biceps femoris — long head
cards.etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’; ‘long head’ is the longer of its two origins. So it is ‘the long head of the two-headed thigh muscle’, starting up at the sitting bone.
cards.origin: Ischial tuberosity (common tendon with semitendinosus)
cards.insertion: Head of the fibula (with the short head)
cards.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
cards.tip: Crosses both hip and knee, so it is the most commonly strained hamstring in sprinting.

cards.name: Biceps femoris — short head
cards.etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’; ‘short head’ is the shorter origin. So it is ‘the short head of the two-headed thigh muscle’, starting on the femur shaft.
cards.origin: Lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur
cards.insertion: Head of the fibula (with the long head)
cards.innervation: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
cards.tip: The only hamstring-group part that doesn’t cross the hip — and the only one supplied by the common fibular division.

cards.name: Brachialis
cards.etymology: From Latin brachialis ‘of the arm’ (brachium, arm). So it simply means ‘the arm muscle’ — the deep flexor lying on the front of the humerus.
cards.origin: Distal half of the anterior surface of the humerus
cards.insertion: Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna
cards.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6); small lateral part by the radial nerve (C7)
cards.tip: The “workhorse” elbow flexor — it inserts on the ulna, so forearm rotation does not change its leverage; hammer and reverse curls emphasise it.

cards.name: Brachioradialis
cards.etymology: From Latin brachium ‘arm’ + radialis ‘of the radius’. So it means ‘the muscle from the arm (humerus) to the radius’.
cards.origin: Proximal two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus
cards.insertion: Lateral surface of the distal radius, just proximal to the radial styloid process
actions: Elbow flexion (strongest with forearm in mid-prone/neutral)
Returns forearm to mid-prone from full pronation or supination
cards.tip: An elbow flexor supplied by the radial (“extensor”) nerve; hammer curls target it and its reflex tests C6.

cards.name: Coracobrachialis
cards.etymology: From Greek korax ‘raven’ (the coracoid process looks like a raven’s beak) + Latin brachium ‘arm’. So it means ‘the muscle from the coracoid to the arm’.
cards.origin: Apex of the coracoid process of scapula (with short head of biceps)
cards.insertion: Middle third of the medial surface of the humerus
cards.tip: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it — a handy landmark in the axilla.

cards.name: External intercostals
cards.etymology: From Latin externus ‘outer’ + inter ‘between’ + costa ‘rib’. So it means ‘the outer muscles between the ribs’ — the outermost of three intercostal layers.
cards.origin: Inferior border of the rib above
cards.insertion: Superior border of the rib below; fibres run down and forward (‘hands in pockets’)
cards.tip: Fibres run like the external oblique; they are the main intercostal inspiratory layer and work hard in heavy breathing.

cards.name: Fibularis brevis
cards.etymology: From Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’ + -aris ‘relating to’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short fibula muscle’.
cards.origin: Lower two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
cards.insertion: Tuberosity on the base of the 5th metatarsal
cards.tip: A forceful inversion sprain can avulse its insertion — a 5th metatarsal base fracture.

cards.name: Fibularis longus
cards.etymology: From Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’ + -aris ‘relating to’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long fibula muscle’ (peroneus from Greek peronē ‘pin’, the same bone).
cards.origin: Head and upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
cards.insertion: Plantar surfaces of the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform (tendon crosses the sole in the cuboid groove)
actions: Supports the lateral longitudinal and transverse arches
cards.tip: With tibialis anterior it forms a ‘stirrup’ under the foot; strengthen the fibularis muscles after lateral ankle sprains.

cards.name: Gastrocnemius — lateral head
cards.etymology: From Greek gastēr ‘belly’ + knēmē ‘leg’, plus Latin lateralis ‘of the side’. So it is ‘the outer head of the leg’s belly muscle’.
cards.origin: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle
cards.insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
cards.tip: Often contains a small sesamoid bone (fabella) in its tendon behind the lateral knee.

cards.name: Gastrocnemius — medial head
cards.etymology: From Greek gastēr ‘belly’ + knēmē ‘leg’, plus Latin medialis ‘of the inner side’. So it is ‘the inner head of the leg’s belly muscle’.
cards.origin: Posterior surface of the femur just above the medial condyle
cards.insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
cards.tip: Larger and lower than the lateral head; ‘tennis leg’ is classically a tear of this head.

cards.name: Gluteus minimus
cards.etymology: From Greek gloutos ‘buttock’ + Latin minimus ‘smallest’. So it means ‘the smallest buttock muscle’ — the deepest of the three glutes.
cards.origin: External surface of ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
cards.insertion: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
actions: Stabilises the pelvis in single-leg stance
cards.tip: Works with glute med as a pelvic stabiliser; its tendon is a common site of lateral hip (greater trochanteric) pain.

cards.name: Gracilis
cards.etymology: From Latin gracilis ‘slender, thin’. So it means ‘the slender muscle’ — a long, strap-like muscle down the inner thigh.
cards.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
cards.insertion: Superior medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
cards.tip: The only adductor crossing the knee; middle tendon of the pes anserinus — ‘Say Grace before Tea’.

cards.name: Iliacus
cards.etymology: From Latin ilium / ilia ‘flank, groin’ (the hip bone’s wing) + -acus ‘belonging to’. So it means ‘the muscle of the ilium’ — it fills the iliac fossa.
cards.origin: Iliac fossa, inner lip of the iliac crest and ala of the sacrum
cards.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (with the psoas major tendon)
cards.tip: Joins psoas major to form the iliopsoas, the strongest hip flexor; tightness pulls the pelvis into anterior tilt.

cards.name: Iliocostalis lumborum
cards.etymology: From Latin ilium ‘flank / hip bone’ + costa ‘rib’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the hip-to-rib muscle of the lower back’ — it runs from the iliac crest up to the ribs.
cards.origin: Common erector spinae tendon: iliac crest, sacrum, lumbar spinous processes and thoracolumbar fascia
cards.insertion: Angles of the lower 6–9 ribs (and transverse processes of upper lumbar vertebrae)
cards.innervation: Dorsal rami of lumbar and lower thoracic spinal nerves
cards.tip: The most lateral erector column — the visible ‘ropes’ beside the spine in deadlift lockout; resists side-bending under load.

cards.name: Infraspinatus
cards.etymology: From Latin infra ‘below’ + spina ‘spine’. So it means ‘the muscle below the spine (of the scapula)’, filling the infraspinous fossa.
cards.origin: Medial two-thirds of the infraspinous fossa of scapula
cards.insertion: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of humerus
actions: Stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid (rotator cuff)
cards.tip: The main external rotator of the cuff — side-lying or cable external rotations target it; suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch weakens it alone.

cards.name: Internal intercostals
cards.etymology: From Latin internus ‘inner’ + inter ‘between’ + costa ‘rib’. So it means ‘the inner muscles between the ribs’ — the middle intercostal layer, deep to the externals.
cards.origin: Inferior border and costal groove of the rib above
cards.insertion: Superior border of the rib below; fibres run down and back, at right angles to the externals
actions: Rib depression during forced expiration (interosseous part)
cards.tip: Active in forced exhalation — e.g. coughing, the end of a hard breath out during bracing or sprinting.

cards.name: Levator scapulae
cards.etymology: From Latin levator ‘lifter’ (levare, to raise) + scapulae ‘of the shoulder blade’. So it means ‘the lifter of the scapula’ — exactly what it does.
cards.origin: Transverse processes of C1–C4 (posterior tubercles of C3–C4)
cards.insertion: Medial border of scapula from superior angle to root of spine
actions: Cervical ipsilateral lateral flexion and rotation
cards.innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and cervical nerves C3–C4
cards.tip: Classic source of ‘knot’ pain at the superior angle of the scapula; stretch with neck flexion + contralateral rotation (nose to opposite armpit).

cards.name: Longissimus thoracis
cards.etymology: From Latin longissimus ‘longest’ (superlative of longus) + thoracis ‘of the chest’. So it means ‘the longest muscle, thoracic part’ — longissimus is the longest erector column.
cards.origin: Common erector spinae tendon (sacrum, iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes) and transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae
cards.insertion: Transverse processes of all thoracic vertebrae, ribs 2/3–12 between tubercles and angles, and lumbar accessory processes
cards.innervation: Dorsal rami of thoracic and lumbar spinal nerves
cards.tip: The largest erector column; a key target in back extensions and the hinge pattern, and often guarded/spasmed in acute low back pain.

cards.name: Masseter
cards.etymology: From Greek masētēr ‘chewer’ (from masasthai ‘to chew’). So it means ‘the chewer’ — the main muscle you feel bulge when chewing.
cards.origin: Superficial part: zygomatic process of maxilla and anterior two-thirds of zygomatic arch; deep part: posterior third and medial surface of zygomatic arch
cards.insertion: Lateral surface of ramus and angle of mandible (deep part higher, up to coronoid process)
cards.tip: Strongest muscle for its size; often tender in bruxism and TMJ dysfunction — palpate at the angle of the jaw while clenching.

cards.name: Multifidus lumborum
cards.etymology: From Latin multus ‘many’ + findere ‘to split’ (-fidus, split) + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘split into many parts, of the low back’ — many short bundles fanning between vertebrae.
cards.origin: Dorsal sacrum, posterior superior iliac spine, erector spinae aponeurosis and mammillary processes of lumbar vertebrae
cards.insertion: Spinous processes 2–4 segments above
cards.innervation: Medial branches of dorsal rami of lumbar spinal nerves (each fascicle by the nerve of its own level)
cards.tip: Atrophies and gets fatty infiltration on the painful side in low back pain and does not recover spontaneously — targeted motor-control training is key.

cards.name: Pectineus
cards.etymology: From Latin pecten ‘comb’. So it means ‘the comb muscle’ — it arises from the pecten pubis, a comb-like ridge on the pubic bone.
cards.origin: Pecten pubis (pectineal line of the superior pubic ramus)
cards.insertion: Pectineal line of the femur, just below the lesser trochanter
cards.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2–L3); sometimes a branch of the obturator nerve
cards.tip: Forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle and is often strained along with adductor longus in groin injuries.

cards.name: Pectoralis major — sternocostal head
cards.etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger chest muscle’ (vs pectoralis minor beneath it). ‘Sternocostal’ is from Greek sternon ‘chest, breastbone’ + Latin costa ‘rib’ — the head arising from the sternum and rib cartilages.
cards.origin: Anterior surface of sternum and costal cartilages 1–6
cards.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
actions: Shoulder extension from a flexed position
cards.tip: The bulk of the pec — flat and decline pressing, dips and high-to-low flyes load it most.

cards.name: Pectoralis minor
cards.etymology: From Latin pectoralis ‘of the chest’ (pectus, breast) + minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller chest muscle’, lying under pectoralis major.
cards.origin: Anterior surfaces of ribs 3–5 near their costal cartilages
cards.insertion: Medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of scapula
actions: Elevates ribs 3–5 in forced inspiration (scapula fixed)
cards.innervation: Medial pectoral nerve (C8–T1), with a contribution from the lateral pectoral nerve
cards.tip: A short pec minor tilts the scapula forward (rounded shoulders) and can compress the brachial plexus beneath it (pectoralis minor / thoracic outlet syndrome).

cards.name: Piriformis
cards.etymology: From Latin pirum ‘pear’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘pear-shaped’ — a flat, tapering muscle passing out of the greater sciatic notch.
cards.origin: Anterior surface of the sacrum (S2–S4 level) and margin of the greater sciatic notch
cards.insertion: Superior border of the greater trochanter
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
cards.tip: The sciatic nerve usually exits just below it (sometimes through it), so a tight piriformis can mimic sciatica — ‘piriformis syndrome’.

cards.name: Platysma
cards.etymology: From Greek platysma ‘a flat plate’, from platys ‘broad, flat’. So it means ‘the flat sheet’ — a thin, broad sheet of muscle lying in the skin of the neck.
cards.origin: Superficial fascia over upper pectoralis major and deltoid
cards.insertion: Inferior border of mandible, skin of lower face and angle of mouth (modiolus)
actions: Depresses the angle of the mouth and lower lip
Tenses the skin of the neck (grimace)
cards.tip: A facial-expression muscle in the neck — so it is supplied by CN VII, not a cervical spinal nerve.

cards.name: Psoas major
cards.etymology: From Greek psoa ‘loin muscles’ + Latin major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger loin muscle’ — the long muscle running from the lumbar spine down to the thigh.
cards.origin: Sides of the T12–L5 vertebral bodies and intervening discs; transverse processes of L1–L5
cards.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (with iliacus)
cards.tip: With iliacus it forms the iliopsoas; a tight psoas increases lumbar lordosis — test with the Thomas test.

cards.name: Quadratus lumborum
cards.etymology: From Latin quadratus ‘squared, four-sided’ + lumborum ‘of the loins’. So it means ‘the square muscle of the low back’ — a rectangular sheet between the 12th rib and the iliac crest.
cards.origin: Posterior iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament
cards.insertion: Medial half of inferior border of 12th rib and transverse processes of L1–L4
actions: Pelvic elevation (‘hip hiking’) on the same side
cards.tip: Hikes the hip in gait (and compensates for weak glute med); suitcase carries and side planks train it as a lateral stabiliser.

cards.name: Rhomboid major
cards.etymology: From Greek rhombos ‘rhombus / spinning top’ + eidos ‘shape’, via Latin; major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger rhombus-shaped muscle’ — a flat parallelogram between spine and scapula.
cards.origin: Spinous processes of T2–T5 and supraspinous ligaments
cards.insertion: Medial border of scapula, from root of spine to inferior angle
cards.tip: Works with middle trap in rows; weakness lets the scapula ‘wing’ at its medial border and drift into protraction.

cards.name: Rhomboid minor
cards.etymology: From Greek rhombos ‘rhombus’ + eidos ‘shape’; minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller rhombus-shaped muscle’, sitting just above rhomboid major.
cards.origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7–T1
cards.insertion: Medial border of scapula at the root (base) of the scapular spine
cards.tip: Functionally identical to rhomboid major — trained with rows, face pulls and scapular retraction drills.

cards.name: Sartorius
cards.etymology: From Latin sartor ‘tailor’ (from sarcire ‘to patch, mend’). So it means ‘the tailor’s muscle’ — it produces the cross-legged position tailors sat in to sew.
cards.origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
cards.insertion: Superior medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
cards.tip: Longest muscle in the body; pes anserinus order front-to-back is Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus — ‘Say Grace before Tea’.

cards.name: Subscapularis
cards.etymology: From Latin sub ‘under’ + scapula ‘shoulder blade’. So it means ‘the muscle under (on the front of) the shoulder blade’, filling the subscapular fossa.
cards.origin: Subscapular fossa (anterior surface of scapula)
cards.insertion: Lesser tubercle of humerus (and anterior shoulder capsule)
actions: Stabilises the humeral head anteriorly (rotator cuff)
cards.tip: The only rotator cuff muscle on the lesser tubercle (the “S” facing forward in SITS); test with the lift-off or belly-press test.

cards.name: Supraspinatus
cards.etymology: From Latin supra ‘above’ + spina ‘spine’. So it means ‘the muscle above the spine (of the scapula)’, filling the supraspinous fossa.
cards.origin: Medial two-thirds of the supraspinous fossa of scapula
cards.insertion: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of humerus
actions: Stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid (rotator cuff)
cards.tip: Rotator cuff = SITS (Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis); supraspinatus is the most commonly impinged and torn — test with empty/full can.

cards.name: Temporalis
cards.etymology: From Latin tempora ‘the temples’ (plural of tempus, which also means ‘time’ — probably because grey hair first shows there). So it means ‘the muscle of the temple’.
cards.origin: Floor of temporal fossa and deep surface of temporal fascia
cards.insertion: Coronoid process and anterior border of ramus of mandible
cards.tip: Palpate at the temple while clenching; trigger points here commonly refer pain as temporal headache and with jaw clenching/bruxism.

cards.name: Tensor fasciae latae
cards.etymology: From Latin tensor ‘stretcher, tightener’ + fasciae ‘of the band’ + latae ‘broad’. So it means ‘tightener of the broad band’ — it tenses the fascia lata / IT band.
cards.origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and anterior part of the outer iliac crest
cards.insertion: Iliotibial tract, which attaches to the lateral tibial condyle (Gerdy’s tubercle)
actions: Tenses the IT tract to stabilise the extended knee
cards.tip: Often overactive when glute med is weak; tightness is linked to IT band syndrome on the lateral knee.

cards.name: Teres major
cards.etymology: From Latin teres ‘round, smooth (rounded off)’ + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger round muscle’ (vs teres minor above it).
cards.origin: Dorsal surface of the inferior angle of scapula
cards.insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
cards.tip: NOT part of the rotator cuff — it is “lat’s little helper”; mnemonic: “a lady between two majors” (lat dorsi inserts between pec major and teres major).

cards.name: Teres minor
cards.etymology: From Latin teres ‘round, smooth (rounded off)’ + minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller round muscle’ (vs teres major below it).
cards.origin: Upper two-thirds of the posterior surface of the lateral border of scapula
cards.insertion: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of humerus
actions: Stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid (rotator cuff)
cards.tip: A rotator cuff muscle (SITS) supplied by the axillary nerve, not the suprascapular; the hornblower’s sign tests it.

cards.name: Triceps brachii — lateral head
cards.etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘lateral head’ lies on the outer side of the back of the arm.
cards.origin: Posterior surface of humerus, superior (lateral) to the radial groove
cards.insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (common tendon)
cards.tip: Gives the “horseshoe” shape on the outer arm; pushdowns with a neutral grip load it well.

cards.name: Triceps brachii — long head
cards.etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘long head’ is the longest, arising from the scapula and crossing the shoulder.
cards.origin: Infraglenoid tubercle of scapula
cards.insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (common tendon)
cards.tip: The only biarticular head — overhead extensions and pullovers stretch it; it forms borders of the quadrangular and triangular spaces.

cards.name: Triceps brachii — medial head
cards.etymology: From Latin tri- ‘three’ + caput ‘head’ (triceps, ‘three-headed’) + brachii ‘of the arm’ (brachium). So it means ‘the three-headed muscle of the arm’. The ‘medial head’ lies deep and toward the inner side, below the radial groove.
cards.origin: Posterior surface of humerus, inferior (medial) to the radial groove
cards.insertion: Posterior surface of the olecranon process of ulna (common tendon) and elbow joint capsule
actions: Elbow extension (active in all extension, even low load)
cards.tip: The workhorse of elbow extension; the radial nerve runs in the groove between it and the lateral head — at risk in humeral shaft fractures.

cards.name: Vastus intermedius
cards.etymology: From Latin vastus ‘vast, huge’ + intermedius ‘lying between’. So it means ‘the huge muscle in between’ — it lies deep, between the other two vasti, under rectus femoris.
cards.origin: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft (upper two-thirds)
cards.insertion: Deep surface of the quadriceps tendon to the patella, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
cards.tip: Hidden under rectus femoris; a small slip from it (articularis genus) lifts the knee joint capsule during extension.

cards.name: 10th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The tenth costa — the last false rib and atypical.
articulations: T10 body (costovertebral joint — usually a single facet on the head)
landmarks: Usually a single facet on the head
Tubercle, angle and costal groove present
Forms the lowest point of the costal margin
cards.tip: The lowest point of the costal margin, at the 10th costal cartilage, marks the subcostal plane (about L3).

cards.name: 11th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The eleventh costa — a floating rib (vertebral) and atypical.
articulations: Anterior end free in the abdominal wall muscles
landmarks: No tubercle (no articulation with the transverse process); neck indistinct
Slight angle and shallow costal groove
cards.tip: A floating rib — its tip ends in the abdominal wall, so it has no anterior attachment.

cards.name: 1st metacarpal (thumb)
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm. This one supports the thumb.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the thumb (MCP joint)
landmarks: Insertion of opponens pollicis (shaft) and abductor pollicis longus (base)
Two sesamoids at the palmar head
cards.tip: A fracture-dislocation of its base is a Bennett’s fracture; it lies in a different plane, letting the thumb oppose.

cards.name: 1st metatarsal (big toe)
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the big toe (MTP joint)
Medial and lateral sesamoids (under the head)
landmarks: Tuberosity on the plantar base (fibularis longus)
Grooves under the head for the two sesamoids
cards.tip: Takes the most load at push-off; hallux valgus (bunion) angles its head medially.

cards.name: 2nd metacarpal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the index finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Insertion of extensor carpi radialis longus (dorsal base) and flexor carpi radialis (palmar base)
cards.tip: Its keyed-in base makes the index CMC joint almost immobile — the stable post of the hand.

cards.name: 2nd metatarsal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 2nd toe (MTP joint)
landmarks: Base recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms
Lisfranc ligament attachment (from the medial cuneiform)
cards.tip: Its rigid, keyed-in base makes it the classic site of a metatarsal stress (‘march’) fracture.

cards.name: 2nd rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The second costa — a true rib and atypical.
articulations: Sternum at the sternal angle via its costal cartilage
landmarks: About twice the length of rib 1, thinner and less curved
Tuberosity for serratus anterior on its outer surface
cards.tip: Its cartilage meets the sternal angle — the first rib you can reliably count from the front.

cards.name: 3rd metacarpal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Styloid process on the dorsal base
Insertion of extensor carpi radialis brevis (base)
Origin of adductor pollicis (transverse head, shaft)
cards.tip: The only metacarpal with a styloid process, where ECRB inserts; with the 2nd it forms the rigid central column.

cards.name: 3rd metatarsal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 3rd toe (MTP joint)
cards.tip: Also a common stress-fracture site; with the 2nd it forms the stiff central forefoot.

cards.name: 3rd rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The third costa — a true rib (vertebrosternal) and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
cards.tip: Pectoralis minor arises from ribs 3–5 — a tight pec minor tilts the scapula forward.

cards.name: 4th metacarpal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Small quadrilateral base with facets for capitate and hamate
cards.tip: Its CMC joint is mobile, letting the ulnar side of the palm cup for grip.

cards.name: 4th metatarsal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 4th toe (MTP joint)
landmarks: Quadrilateral base articulating with the cuboid
cards.tip: Part of the mobile lateral column — its joint with the cuboid lets the outer forefoot adapt to the ground.

cards.name: 4th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The fourth costa — a true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Origin of pectoralis minor (ribs 3–5) and serratus anterior slips
cards.tip: In men the nipple usually lies over the 4th intercostal space, just below this rib.

cards.name: 5th metacarpal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the little finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Tubercle on the medial base (extensor carpi ulnaris)
cards.tip: A punch with a closed fist commonly breaks its neck — the ‘boxer’s fracture’.

cards.name: 5th metatarsal
cards.etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 5th toe (MTP joint)
landmarks: Tuberosity on the lateral base (fibularis brevis)
Origin of flexor digiti minimi brevis
cards.tip: An inversion sprain can avulse its tuberosity; a Jones fracture is just beyond, at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, and heals poorly.

cards.name: 5th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The fifth costa — a true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Costal cartilage receives part of rectus abdominis (cartilages 5–7)
cards.tip: The apex beat of the heart is felt in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line — just below this rib.

cards.name: 6th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The sixth costa — a true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage gives origin to the sternocostal head of pectoralis major (cartilages 1–6) and part of rectus abdominis
cards.tip: Intercostal nerves run in the costal groove under each rib — needles go just above a rib, never below.

cards.name: 7th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The seventh costa — the last true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum near the xiphisternal junction via its costal cartilage
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage gives insertion to rectus abdominis
cards.tip: The last rib whose own cartilage reaches the sternum (ribs 1–7 are ‘true’ ribs).

cards.name: 8th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The eighth costa — the first false rib (vertebrochondral) and typical.
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage forms part of the costal margin
cards.tip: Its cartilage joins the one above rather than the sternum — the first ‘false’ rib; cartilages 7–10 form the costal margin.

cards.name: 9th rib
cards.etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The ninth costa — a false rib (vertebrochondral) and typical.
landmarks: Last typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage forms part of the costal margin
cards.tip: Lower-rib fractures (8–12) on the right can injure the liver, on the left the spleen.

cards.name: C3 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the third neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C2 and C4
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
cards.tip: C3 sits behind the hyoid bone — the first typical cervical vertebra below the specialised C1–C2 pair.

cards.name: C4 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the fourth neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C3 and C5
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
Level of the upper thyroid cartilage / carotid bifurcation
cards.tip: C4 lies roughly at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, where the common carotid artery usually bifurcates; the C4 root helps form the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

cards.name: C5 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the fifth neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C4 and C6
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
cards.tip: C5–C6 is the most common level for cervical disc degeneration; the C5 root (deltoid, biceps) exits above C5.

cards.name: C6 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the sixth neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C5 and C7
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
Carotid tubercle (enlarged anterior tubercle of transverse process)
cards.tip: C6 has the prominent carotid (Chassaignac’s) tubercle — the common carotid can be compressed against it; level of the cricoid cartilage, where larynx becomes trachea and pharynx becomes oesophagus.

cards.name: Capitate
cards.etymology: From Latin caput ‘head’ (capitatus ‘having a head’). So it means ‘the bone with a head’ — its rounded head fits into the lunate and scaphoid. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
cards.tip: The largest and most central carpal — the axis around which wrist movement is often described; aligned with the 3rd metacarpal.

cards.name: Cuboid
cards.etymology: From Greek kybos ‘cube’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘cube-shaped bone’. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Groove for the fibularis (peroneus) longus tendon
cards.tip: Fibularis longus runs in its plantar groove on the way to the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform.

cards.name: Ethmoid bone
cards.etymology: From Greek ēthmos ‘sieve’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘sieve-like bone’ — its cribriform plate is perforated like a sieve for the olfactory nerve fibres.
cards.tip: A fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell and CSF leaking from the nose.

cards.name: Hamate
cards.etymology: From Latin hamatus ‘hooked’, from hamus ‘hook’. So it means ‘the hooked bone’ — named for the hook projecting from its palmar surface. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
cards.tip: The hook can fracture from the butt of a golf club, bat or racket pressing into the palm.

cards.name: Intermediate cuneiform
cards.etymology: From Latin cuneus ‘wedge’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch like wedges in a Roman arch. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Set back (recessed) so the 2nd metatarsal base keys in between the medial and lateral cuneiforms
cards.tip: Its recessed position locks the 2nd metatarsal base — the keystone of the Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) joint.

cards.name: L1 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the first vertebra of the loin (low back).
landmarks: Kidney-shaped body, no costal facets or transverse foramina
cards.tip: In adults the spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually ends at L1–L2; the transpyloric plane crosses L1.

cards.name: L2 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the second vertebra of the loin (low back).
landmarks: Attachment of the diaphragmatic crura (right L1–L3, left L1–L2)
cards.tip: Psoas major arises from the bodies and transverse processes of T12–L4/L5, including L2; L2 is in the middle of its origin.

cards.name: L3 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the third vertebra of the loin (low back).
cards.tip: Sits at the apex of the lumbar lordosis; its long transverse processes are a big lever for quadratus lumborum and the thoracolumbar fascia.

cards.name: L4 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the fourth vertebra of the loin (low back).
landmarks: Spinous process level with the tops of the iliac crests (supracristal plane, L4 or L4–L5)
cards.tip: Draw a line between the iliac crest tops to find L4 — the usual landmark for lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5; the aorta bifurcates at L4.

cards.name: Lateral cuneiform
cards.etymology: From Latin cuneus ‘wedge’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch like wedges in a Roman arch. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Origin of part of flexor hallucis brevis
cards.tip: Sits between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, linking the medial and lateral columns of the foot.

cards.name: Lunate
cards.etymology: From Latin luna ‘moon’. So it means ‘moon-shaped bone’ — it is crescent-shaped. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Concave distal surface for the capitate
cards.tip: The most commonly dislocated carpal (can compress the median nerve); avascular necrosis of it is Kienböck’s disease.

cards.name: Medial cuneiform
cards.etymology: From Latin cuneus ‘wedge’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch like wedges in a Roman arch. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Insertion of tibialis anterior and fibularis longus (with base of 1st metatarsal)
Lisfranc ligament attachment (to the 2nd metatarsal base)
cards.tip: Tibialis anterior and fibularis longus insert side by side on it, acting like a stirrup under the medial arch.

cards.name: Navicular
cards.etymology: From Latin navicula ‘little boat’, diminutive of navis ‘ship’. So it means ‘boat-shaped bone’. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Concave proximal surface for the talar head
Three facets distally for the cuneiforms
cards.tip: Its tuberosity is palpable in front of the medial malleolus — the landmark for the navicular drop test of arch collapse.

cards.name: Pisiform
cards.etymology: From Latin pisum ‘pea’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘pea-shaped bone’ — small and round. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Sesamoid within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
cards.tip: The bony pea you can feel at the base of the hypothenar eminence; FCU pulls through it via the pisohamate/pisometacarpal ligaments.

cards.name: T1 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the first chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 1.
articulations: Rib 1 head (full facet) and rib 2 head (demifacet)
landmarks: Full (whole) superior costal facet for the head of rib 1
Cervical-like body with small uncinate lips
cards.tip: T1’s spinous process is often as prominent as C7’s; its full facet for rib 1 makes it unique among the upper thoracic vertebrae.

cards.name: T10 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the tenth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 10.
articulations: Tubercle of rib 10 (costotransverse joint, when present)
landmarks: Usually a single whole costal facet for rib 10 (body/pedicle junction)
Transverse costal facet small or absent
cards.tip: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm at about the T10 level.

cards.name: T11 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the eleventh chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 11.
landmarks: Single whole costal facet for rib 11 on the pedicle
No transverse costal facet (rib 11 has no tubercle articulation)
cards.tip: A transitional vertebra: no transverse-process rib joint, so rotation starts to be restricted.

cards.name: T12 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the twelfth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 12.
landmarks: Single whole costal facet for rib 12
Thoracic-type superior and lumbar-type inferior articular processes
cards.tip: The thoracolumbar junction — a common site of osteoporotic compression fractures; the aorta passes through the diaphragm at T12.

cards.name: T2 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the second chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 2.
cards.tip: The jugular (suprasternal) notch lies at about the T2–T3 level.

cards.name: T3 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the third chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 3.
cards.tip: The T3 spinous process is level with the root of the spine of the scapula (arms by the sides).

cards.name: T4 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the fourth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 4.
cards.tip: The sternal angle lines up with the T4–T5 disc — the plane of the tracheal bifurcation and the start and end of the aortic arch.

cards.name: T5 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the fifth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 5.
landmarks: Body may be flattened on the left by the descending aorta
cards.tip: Typical mid-thoracic vertebra: steep, overlapping spinous processes limit extension in this region.

cards.name: T6 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the sixth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 6.
landmarks: Heart-shaped body, long downward-sloping spinous process
cards.tip: The textbook ‘typical’ thoracic vertebra — its spinous tip lies over the body of the vertebra below.

cards.name: T7 vertebra
cards.etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the seventh chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 7.
cards.tip: The inferior angle of the scapula sits level with the T7 spinous process (arms by the sides) — a handy counting landmark.

cards.name: T8 vertebra
